excerpts.text: Full bathroom waterproofing and re-tiling — total S$2,000 (inclusive of materials).
Works to be completed by 15 July 2026.
Received with thanks S$2,000.00 from Tan Wei Ling. 20 June 2026.
[12 Jul] Sorry ah, supplier delay on the tiles. Can we push to end of the month? Will finish by 29 Jul.
4. Delays caused by material supply are not within the contractor's control.
5. Any change to the agreed completion date is to be confirmed in writing.
20 Aug   PAYNOW REFUND  PRECISION HOME REPAIRS   +400.00
[18 Aug] Ms Tan, we can come back and finish the tiling at no extra charge. Waterproofing already done and the floor tiles are laid. Or we refund you part, up to you.
[20 Aug] Ok. Refunded $400 today. Sorry again.
[Reading stopped at page 100 of 120. The remaining pages were not read.]

facts.statement: Precision Home Repairs quoted S$2,000 for bathroom waterproofing and re-tiling, and Tan Wei Ling accepted.
Tan Wei Ling paid S$2,000 on 20 June 2026.
The work was to be completed by 15 July 2026.
On 12 July the contractor asked to move the completion date to 29 July. Whether Tan Wei Ling agreed is not established.
As at 28 August 2026 the re-tiling was not finished.
Tan Wei Ling paid Kim Seng Renovation S$500 on 28 August 2026 to finish the work.
Refund of S$2,500. This does not account for the S$400 already refunded, or the S$300 cash paid on 2 June.
Tan Wei Ling paid S$300 in cash to Ah Seng on 2 June 2026.
The contractor says the waterproofing was completed and the floor tiles laid, with the wall tiling outstanding.
The contractor refunded S$400 on 20 August 2026.
On 18 August the contractor offered to complete the tiling at no extra charge, or to refund part of the price.

openQuestions.question: On 12 July the contractor asked to move the date to 29 July. What did you reply?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: If a later date was agreed, the deadline that matters changes. If it was not, the original 15 July date stands. Right now the record does not show which happened.

openQuestions.question: What did the S$500 pay for, and do you have an invoice, receipt, or bank record for it?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Right now this amount rests on your account alone. A record would let you show what was spent and why.

openQuestions.question: Have you asked the contractor for a refund, and what did they say?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: The tribunal process expects parties to have tried to resolve things. It also affects which next steps make sense for you.

openQuestions.question: Has the contractor given a reason for the delay beyond the tile supplier?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Understanding their account helps you prepare for what they may say, rather than being surprised by it.

issues.label: What was agreed, and on what terms
issues.reason: The accepted quote states the scope and the price, and nothing in the other material contradicts it.
issues.nextQuestion: Is the business name on the quote the party you dealt with?

issues.label: What you did under the agreement
issues.reason: The receipt shows S$2,000, and the bank statement shows a further S$300 paid in cash on 2 June. The total paid appears to be S$2,300, which does not match the amount in your account of what happened.
issues.nextQuestion: Was the S$300 on 2 June part of this job, or something separate?
contraryExplanations: The S$300 may have been for a different job, in which case it does not belong in this claim.

issues.label: What the other side did, and by when
issues.reason: The quote gives 15 July, and clause 5 requires any change to be confirmed in writing — which does not appear to have happened. But clause 4 of the same quote says supply delays are outside the contractor's control, and on 18 August the contractor said the waterproofing and floor tiling were done.
issues.nextQuestion: Which parts of the bathroom were finished when you brought in the second contractor?
contraryExplanations: The contractor may rely on clause 4 of their own quote, which you uploaded, to say the tile delay was not their fault.
The contractor may say the work was substantially complete and only the wall tiling remained.
The contractor may say your 'ok' on 12 July agreed the new date.

issues.label: What went wrong
issues.reason: That the work was unfinished rests on your account, and the contractor's message of 18 August describes it differently. We found no photographs or inspection recording the state of the bathroom.
issues.nextQuestion: Do you have photos of the unfinished bathroom, or a message where you told the contractor it was incomplete?
contraryExplanations: The contractor may say the work was substantially complete and only minor items remained.

issues.label: What you lost, and what you are asking for
issues.reason: The S$500 to the second contractor is now supported by your bank statement. But the same statement shows S$400 refunded to you on 20 August, and the S$2,500 you are asking for does not account for it.
issues.nextQuestion: Do you want to claim S$2,500, or the amount you are actually out of pocket after the refund?
contraryExplanations: The contractor will point to the S$400 refund as partial settlement.
The contractor may say the S$500 covered work beyond what they had quoted for.

issues.label: What the other side might say
issues.reason: The record now contains several things the other side is likely to rely on: their own quote's clause about supply delays, an offer to finish at no charge, and a partial refund you accepted.
issues.nextQuestion: What did you say when they offered to finish the tiling for free?
contraryExplanations: Refusing an offer to complete at no charge may be raised against you.
Accepting the S$400 refund may be characterised as partial settlement.

contradictions.description: The quote sets a completion date of 15 July 2026. A chat message on 12 July asks to move it to 29 July. It is not established whether that change was agreed.

alternatives.reading: The deadline stayed 15 July and the contractor missed it.
alternatives.distinguishingFact: What 'ok' referred to in the 12 July message — the delay itself, or the new date.

alternatives.reading: The deadline was moved to 29 July by agreement.
alternatives.distinguishingFact: Any later message treating 29 July as the agreed date, from either side.

contradictions.description: The chat records a supplier delay as the reason. That may support the contractor's account rather than yours.
S$400 was refunded on 20 August. The amount being claimed does not deduct it.
The contractor says the waterproofing and floor tiling were completed. The claim describes the work as not done.

alternatives.distinguishingFact: Photographs of the bathroom before the second contractor started.

alternatives.reading: Most of the work was done and only the wall tiling remained.
alternatives.distinguishingFact: The second contractor's invoice, if it itemises what they did.

contradictions.description: S$2,000 by receipt plus S$300 in cash is S$2,300 paid; S$400 was refunded; S$500 went to the second contractor. None of these figures reconcile to the S$2,500 being claimed.
On 18 August the contractor offered to complete the work at no extra charge. The offer was declined.
Clause 4 of the accepted quote says supply delays are outside the contractor's control. This document was uploaded by the claimant.
